items.title: How to Be a Poet: Elizabeth Alexander on the Yin-Yang of Connection and Contradiction
items.description: “The poets (by which I mean all artists) are finally the only people who know the truth about us,” James Baldwin wrote. “Soldiers don’t. Statesmen don’t. Priests don’t. Union leaders don’t. Only poets.” No matter how slant they may tell it, that truth tells us back to ourselves, helps us tell each other what it is like to be alive. items.title: How to Fall in Love Better: A Field Guide to Enlightened Enchantment
items.description: Enchantment, J.R.R. Tolkien believed, is “as necessary for the health and complete functioning of the Human as is sunlight for physical life.” But enchantment is a story we tell ourselves that tells us back to ourselves, and like every story, it can be true or false. Love is the most powerful enchantment we know, the most transformative if true and the most dangerous if false. “When we are falsely enchanted, we desire either to possess the enchanting being or be possessed by it,” W.H. items.title: Edward Abbey on How to Live and How to Die
items.description: The summer after graduating high school, knowing he would face conscription into the military as soon as his eighteenth birthday arrived, Edward Abbey (January 29, 1927–March 14, 1989) set out to get to know the land he was being asked to die for. He hitchhiked and hopped freight trains, rode in ramshackle busses and walked sweltering miles across the American Southwest. items.title: Emerson on How to Trust Yourself
items.description: "It is easy in solitude to live after our own; but the great man is he who in the midst of the crowd keeps with perfect sweetness the independence of solitude."

items.title: The Vampire Problem: The Paradoxical Psychology of Why It Is So Hard to Change
items.description: "Many of [life's] big decisions involve choices to have experiences that teach us things we cannot know about from any other source but the experience itself."

items.title: Are You Working: In Defense of the Invisible Labors of Creativitiy
items.description: Once, at the gym with a physicist friend, I was struck by how no one else in the room had any idea that while she was sweating on the treadmill with a blank stare into space, she was doing advanced mathematics working out the logic of black holes. items.title: The Three Elements of the Good Life

items.title: Against the Cartesian Myth of Work/Life Balance: André Gregory’s Extraordinary Letter to Richard Avedon about the Nature of Creativity
items.description: Half a millennium into our recovery from the civilizational wound Descartes inflicted by severing the body and the mind, we are bleeding with a Cartesian cleft of our own making — the damaging divide between life and work. The notion of a “workaholic,” often worn as a badge on the lapel of the modern ego, presupposes someone who makes work the central axis of life at the expense of living. items.title: Dostoyevsky, Just After His Death Sentence Was Repealed, on the Meaning of Life
items.description: "To be a human being among people and to remain one forever, no matter in what circumstances, not to grow despondent and not to lose heart — that’s what life is all about, that's its task."

items.title: A Stoic’s Key to Peace of Mind: Seneca on the Antidote to Anxiety
items.description: "There are more things ... likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality."

items.title: Steinbeck and the Difficult Art of the Friend Breakup
items.description: "I can’t consider you a friend when out of every contact there comes some intentionally wounding thing."

items.title: The Science of Waiting and the Art of Delay
items.description: Exploring the intersection of time and decision-making to shine a light on what it means to be human.

items.title: The Courage to Be Yourself: E.E. Cummings on Art, Life, and Being Unafraid to Feel
items.description: "To be nobody-but-yourself — in a world which is doing its best, night and day, to make you everybody else — means to fight the hardest battle which any human being can fight."

items.title: The Stoic Key to Living with Presence: Seneca on Time Spent vs. Saved vs. Wasted
items.description: "Lay hold of to-day’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow’s. While we are postponing, life speeds by. Nothing... is ours, except time."
